The Office is respectfully requested to reconsider and withdraw the rejections in view of the amendments and remarks contained herein. INTERVIEW REQUEST

Applicant respectfully requests an interview with the Examiner of all the presently pending claims that are not found to be in condition for allowance, prior to the mailing of any further Office Actions.

The Office has asserted that the claims are interpreted under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. §112, sixth paragraph, because it uses a generic placeholder coupled with functional language without reciting sufficient structure to achieve the function.

Applicant notes that, "a claim limitation that does not use the term "means" or "step" will trigger the rebuttable presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph does not apply." See, MPEP 2181(1) (emphasis added, internal citations omitted). Applicant notes that none of the claims use the terms "means" or "step." Thus, the presumption is that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph does not apply to the claims.

"When a claim term lacks the word "means," the presumption can be overcome ... if ... the claim term fails to "recite sufficiently definite structure" or else recites "function without reciting sufficient structure for performing that function." See, Williamson v. Citrix

Online, LLC, 792 F.3d 1339, 1349, 115 USPQ2d 1105, 1111 (Fed. Cir. 2015) (en banc) (quoting Watts v. XL Systems, Inc., 232 F.3d 877, 880 (Fed. Cir. 2000). Applicant respectfully submits that the Office's conclusory statement that cited terms are "generic placeholders" (See, Office Action pgs. 2-4) clearly does not meet the required showing that the terms selected by Applicant are a "nonce word" that is not recognized as the name of structure or a "function without reciting sufficient structure for performing that function." See, Id.

Nonetheless, in the interest of expediting prosecution, Applicant notes that MPEP 2181(I)(A) lists non-structural generic placeholders that may invoke §112, sixth paragraph, and none of the provided examples are included in the presently pending claims followed by the word "for". Further, each of the ten non-structural terms listed in MPEP 2181 are constructed from a noun followed by the preposition "for", which directly parallels the "means for" trigger phrase. If the preposition "for" was unimportant, MPEP 2181 would not have included "for" in each of the listed non-structural terms. Therefore, Applicant respectfully submits that there is a substantive distinction between the Office's asserted non-structural terms and the terms actually used by Applicant.

For at least these reasons, Applicant respectfully submits that the presumption against interpreting under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. §112, sixth paragraph has not been overcome, and therefore the various claim terms cited in the Office Action on pgs. 2-4 should not be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. §112, sixth paragraph.

A proper rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 103 includes a finding of each of the claim limitations found in some form within the body of prior art imputed to a person of or having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA), with the additional question of whether it would have been obvious to the PHOSITA to combine the cited references to form the claimed invention. In KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., the Supreme Court wrote that "it can be important to identify a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill in the art to combine the elements as the new invention does". See, KSR Int' Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398, 401 (2007). Extending that decision, the Federal Circuit has ruled that a proper rejection also include (1) a stated reason why a PHOSITA would combine the prior art references; (2) have an adequate evidentiary basis for the asserted reason to combine; and (3) provide a reasonable explanation that includes an express and rational connection with evidence presented for the finding. See, e.g., In re Sang-Su Lee, 277 F.3d 1338, 1345 (Fed. Cir. 2002) ("The board cannot rely on conclusory statements when dealing with particular combinations of prior art and specific claims, but must set forth the rationale on which it relies."); Cutsforth, Inc. v. MotivePower, Inc., 636 Fed. Appx. 575, 578 (Fed. Cir. 2016) ("Board must explain why a person of ordinary skill in the art would modify the prior art references to create the claimed invention".); and Arendi S.A.R.L. v. Apple Inc., 832 F.3d 1355, 1366-67 (Fed. Cir. 2016) (""common sense" was conclusory and unsupported by substantial evidence . . . we reverse the Board's finding of unpatentability.").

Grissom is directed to medical treatments that can induce temperatures above 1000 Celsius that can create steam or bubbles to be formed. When these bubbles or steam is formed, MR signals in this region disappears causing disturbances to appear in

the tissue surrounding the bubble based on a difference in the magnetic susceptibility between air and tissue. This situation may cause safety concerns based on the MR images. Grissom, simply notes that bubbles may be formed because of increased temperatures and these bubbles can cause disturbance to MR images to create safety concerns. Grissom, as acknowledged by the Office does not disclose determining a tracked location of an instrument, accessing a current image of the subject or registering image space of the image to subject space, determining a location of the instrument within the image space, or determining a region of interest relative the determined location of the instrument in the image space.

For these teachings, the Office turns to Jenkins. Jenkins discloses an MRI guided surgical system. As noted in paragraph 91 of Jenkins and referred to by the Office, Jenkins discloses that a fiducial marker can be attached to an intra body device. Such a fiducial marker can be a coating, a shape of a tool, or a tracking member that are "MRI- visible" when detected by the MR scanner. The MR scanner is a magnetic resonance imaging system. Thus, Jenkins clearly discloses using an MRI imaging system to determine where a tool is located but does not disclose tracking a location of an instrument with a tracking system that is separate from an imaging system as set forth in Applicant's independent claim 1 and similarly in claims 12 and 18.

Moreover, Grissom and/or Jenkins, further do not teach analyzing image data of a current image at least with a bubble image library to determine if a bubble is present in the current image within the region of interest, where the bubble image library includes both magnitude images and phase images as also now set forth in Applicant's independent claims 1, 12 and 18. As such, Applicant respectively submits that Grissom

Rinott is directed to a system for correcting measurement artifacts in MR thermometry. Spigelman is directed to an imaging system that is used for surgical procedures performed with respect to a breast of a patient. Here again, however, Rinott nor Spiegelman address any of the deficiencies noted above with regard to Grissom and Jenkins. Accordingly, Rinott and/or Spigelman in combination with Grissom and Jenkins, further do not render obvious Applicant's independent claims 1, 12 and 18 along with Applicant's corresponding dependent claims.
As such, it is respectfully requested that the above rejections be withdrawn, the application be passed to allowance at the Examiner's earliest convenience.
